value.overview: The Coppery-headed Emerald is a tiny hummingbird endemic to Costa Rica. It is associated mainly with humid highland forests, where it visits flowering plants in forest interiors, edges, clearings, and nearby gardens. Males are especially striking because of their metallic copper crown and rump, while females are more subtly marked. Although restricted to one country, it remains fairly common in suitable habitat and occurs in several protected mountain areas.
value.classification: The Coppery-headed Emerald belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the emerald group of tribe Trochilini. Its scientific name is Microchera cupreiceps; it was formerly placed in the genus Elvira.
value.identification: This small hummingbird is about 7.5–8 cm long. The adult male has a brilliant coppery-bronze crown and rump, a green body, and a white undertail area. The female is less brightly colored, with pale underparts and mostly white outer tail feathers marked by a narrow dark band near the tips. Its short bill is noticeably curved downward, a useful feature for separating it from the similar White-tailed Emerald. The species has rapid wingbeats and a compact, energetic appearance.
value.rangeHabitat: The Coppery-headed Emerald occurs only in Costa Rica, chiefly in the northern and central highlands. In Costa Rica it is found mostly on the Caribbean slope of the Cordillera de Guanacaste, Tilarán, and Central mountain ranges, with additional populations on the Pacific slope in the north. It occupies moist to humid montane forest, including both interior and edge habitat, generally from about 700 to 1,500 meters during the breeding period. It also uses clearings, semi-open areas, flowering shrubs, and gardens at suitable elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is a resident species of Costa Rica but makes local altitudinal movements. After breeding, individuals commonly move downslope into lower parts of their range, sometimes reaching about 300 meters; it does not undertake long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Breeding has been recorded mainly from October through March, although timing can vary with local conditions. Males display and sing from perches, often gathering in small leks and chasing rivals. The female builds a small cup nest from plant down and tree-fern material held together with spiderweb, with moss and lichen on the outside. Nests are usually placed in understory vegetation or along forest edges, roughly 1–3 meters above the ground. Clutches normally contain two eggs.
value.dietFeeding: The Coppery-headed Emerald feeds primarily on nectar from a variety of small flowers, shrubs, and trees. Recorded food plants include Besleria, Cavendishia, Clusia, Guarea, Pithecellobium, Quararibea, Satyria, and Inga. It also obtains protein by gleaning small arthropods from leaves and branches or by making short aerial sallies from a perch to catch flying insects. Its short, curved bill is well suited to visiting small flowers.
value.behavior: This active hummingbird forages at several levels of the vegetation. In forest interiors, males are often seen in the canopy, while females more frequently use the understory, although both sexes may occur anywhere in forest edges and clearings. Males defend display or feeding areas and may chase one another during courtship. The species produces high, thin, twittering or warbling song notes and sharp, liquid calls during interactions.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered stable, with an estimated global population of at least 20,000 mature individuals.
